doc.title: James Chirillo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007

title: Jack Peterson, the Fairmont Hotel band and Jerry Bruno; moving to New York
summary: Studying with Jack Peterson, Dallas hotel shows with Jerry Bruno, then West Point band, the 1982 move to New York and a five-year Grand Hyatt job.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: There’s no one guy I can single out, I can name, for different aspects, of being able to stick around and stay alive. As a musician there’s plenty of guys I can name. I went to North Texas in spring, January, whatever, the spring semester but it starts in January of 1975. And I didn’t try out for a jazz band, they’d already pretty much had all that stuff settled from September or whatever, previous. But in the summer, for the summer bands, and I just stayed down there and went to school in the summer, for the summer bands Leon directed it also, but they only had like a band, one band, and it was just from whoever was around. So whoever wanted to like apply, you could end up playing in this band and whatever. So it’s not like you had to really audition for it or nothing. And that first summer I played in that band and that’s when a great guitar player teacher, a guy named Jack Peterson, decided to start teaching at college again. He’s the guy that actually started the guitar program at Berklee back in, I think the late fifties. He really got that going. And he’s an old Texas boy, so he ended moving back down to Dallas and got involved in the whole commercial jingle scene. There was a lot of jingle recording back then in those days, and he was doing everything because he plays great and of course he could arrange like nobody’s business. So then he got tired of doing that and he decided to get back into teaching. So that was that first — so he heard me back then. So I learned a lot from him. I learned a lot from him. And playing at North Texas, they had a band in Dallas at the Fairmont Hotel that actually was it first started, — I forget exactly how that band, how they decided on picking Jerry Gray, but the guy, whoever made that decision, he loved Glenn Miller and Jerry Gray particularly. And he got Jerry Gray to be the band leader at the Fairmont Hotel in Dallas back then, in the early seventies. So he had a great band. Now I think he had just like stopped leading that band right about when I got down there and maybe even had passed away at that time, I’m not really quite sure when Jerry Gray passed away. So I never met him personally. But he’s the guy that got that band going which was a great band. So they’d bring acts in and they didn’t have a steady guitar player, so when they had a show come in, an act come in, that they needed a guitar player, they’d usually try the North Texas guys or whatever, because they could read okay. So I started doing some of those. Joey Heatherton came down and she brought with her her musical director/drummer, a guy named Jerry Fisher, crazy Jerry Fisher — a good guy though, a good drummer — and Jerry Bruno was the bass player. She brought him down. And so Jerry Bruno and I were sitting next to each other for a couple of weeks doing the show and we just sort of hit it off, you know, I mean he played with Frank Sinatra, he played with everybody this guy. He’s still around. He’s in Fort Lee. So we

had a great time. He said, “Man, if you ever come to New York give me a call.” So I ended up saving my money, I ended up joining the Army, in the band, I was in the band at West Point for three years, saved money, moved to New York in 1982, I called up Jerry Bruno and he said come down to the union on Wednesday, you’ll meet whatever, and I’ll introduce you to everybody I know. He introduced me to everybody he knew and a year later just about to the day I realized I had fifty dollars left in the bank. And no money, and a guy that Jerry Bruno had introduced me to called me and offered me a three day a week job at the Grand Hyatt Hotel. And I was there for five years.

Timing, oh yeah. Yeah that’s what you get if you don’t look at the checkbook. I knew I was getting close. So anyway it’s not like I ever had like loads of money but I never really worried about it either.
